extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and applies core patentability standards (novelty, utility, prior user/purchaser rights, and permissible subject-matter). Focuses on when inventions/processes are eligible for patents and defenses to validity under prior use/abandonment rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of purchaser or prior user under the 7th section
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who purchased or used the patented invention prior to the patent being issued, by license, grant, or the consent of the inventor, may claim the benefit of the statute (i.e., a right to use) — but this does not extend to purchasers from a mere wrong-doer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/illustrations: employer who knowingly used the invention under the inventor's consent (or where inventor permitted use while employed) falls within the protection; a purchaser from a fraudster or pirate does not acquire valid title. The statute's remaining clauses (e.g., relating to abandonment and the two-year limit) clarify that the protected purchaser is one who took from the inventor or under his consent. Case law: McClurg v. Kingsland and Pierson v. Eagle Screw Co.; factual inquiry looks to whether prior use/purchase was with inventor's consent or as a license/grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment to the public (defense to patent validity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may be held invalid if there is proof that the invention was abandoned to the public by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the inventor can effect an abandonment to the public; public use without the inventor's knowledge, consent, or sanction does not constitute abandonment. The abandonment exception is carved out of the purchaser/prior-use protection in the statute and limits the inventor's ability to later obtain a patent if he truly abandoned the invention. See related two-year limitation clause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute (worldwide) novelty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be absolutely and not relatively new: it must not have been known or used anywhere in the world, and not described in any public work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is global — prior foreign uses or descriptions can defeat novelty unless other statutory provisos apply. The text emphasizes that novelty relates to every material part of the claimed subject-matter. Courts will examine prior uses/prints worldwide when assessing novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proviso protecting patentees who believed themselves first (foreign prior use exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: If, at the time of applying, the patentee believed himself to be the first inventor/discoverer of the thing patented, the patent shall not be void merely because the thing had been known or used in a foreign country — provided it had not been previously patented or described in a printed publication (or substantial part thereof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory proviso allows an inventor who genuinely thought he was first to take an oath and avoid being debarred by mere foreign secret use or knowledge, so long as no prior foreign patent or printed description exists. The proviso shifts the burden away from secret foreign use unless documented in print or patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication / public work threshold for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as 'described in some public work' or 'described in any printed publication' remains to be judicially defined, but it is suggested that courts would require that the prior description serve as a direction for making or doing the thing described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practical test likely asks whether the prior printed/public description is enabling — i.e., sufficiently instructive to permit making/doing the invention. The precise boundaries of 'public work' and 'printed publication' are open to interpretation by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty must cover every material part; entirety principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelty required relates to every material thing, process, or part of the invention that is represented as a substantial and material part of the subject-matter; novelty is an entirety — if any part fails, the patent is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee was not the original and first inventor or discoverer of a substantial and material part claimed as new, that failure can be a statutory defense. Practical consequence: claims must be novel in all material respects; partial lack of novelty can invalidate the whole patent or the claimed portion depending on statutory remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility and truthful sufficiency (ability to produce described effect)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent contains more than is necessary to produce the described effect and such addition was made to deceive the public, the patent will be invalid; if the whole patent fails to produce the described effect, no action can be maintained upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: stuffing a specification with unnecessary matter intended to mislead or to broaden scope invites invalidation. A patent must be able to produce the described effect (practical utility and sufficiency); failure of the invention to perform as described defeats enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory subject-matter categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters-patent are directed to 'any new and useful art, machine, manufacture or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement' thereof (statutory enumeration of subjects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise proceeds to analyze how those categories have been interpreted; practitioners should map inventions to these statutory buckets and to judicial constructions (e.g., 'manufacture' and 'process' interpretations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that the subject produce an effect in manufactured (corporeal) matter — no patents for abstract principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever the character or description, the result must be an effect produced in manufactured matter; the subject-matter cannot be merely an elementary principle or abstract discovery without practical application to producing a particular effect in matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core rule: patents are intended to promote arts and manufactures, not to create monopolies in abstract scientific principles. A mere principle, rule, or elementary truth in physics is not patentable unless applied practically. This is illustrated by multiple authorities cited in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of things produced vs. modes/processes of production
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject-matter of a patent may be either a tangible thing produced (a manufacture/machine/composition) or the mode (process/method) of producing a thing; 'manufacture' can be construed to include processes and methods when the process embodies a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Watt's 'method of lessening consumption of steam' was upheld as patentable because a principle was embodied in a practical process. Patents for applying gas flame to remove lace fibres, using anthracite with hot air blast in smelting, and a welding mode without a mandril were upheld. When the invention is a process, the patent may cover means/apparatus by which the process can be carried on, provided the inventor both discovered the principle and invented a mode of carrying it into effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principles are patentable only when developed and embodied in a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: A principle, rule, or truth in mechanics or physics cannot be the subject of a patent in the abstract; it becomes patentable only when it is developed, carried out, embodied, and connected with corporeal substances so as to act and produce effects in some art — i.e., when it is reduced to a process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: attempting to claim an abstract principle or a broad method unconfined to producing a particular product/result will be rejected as it would create overbroad monopolies covering every application of the principle. The safe course is to claim the specific mode/means of applying the principle and the practical result thereby achieved.
